content: Chronotype refers to an individual's natural inclination regarding the timing of their daily periods of activity and rest. It determines whether a person is more alert and active in the early hours of the day or later in the evening. This spectrum is often described as morningness or eveningness, with individuals commonly referred to as larks (morning types) or owls (evening types). Morning types tend to wake up early and are most alert during the first part of the day, while evening types are more alert in the evening and prefer to stay up late. Chronotype is also known as circadian type, diurnal preference, or diurnal variation. Humans, as diurnal animals, are naturally active during the daytime, and their activity-rest patterns are regulated by endogenous circadian rhythms. Normal variations in chronotype typically involve sleep-wake cycles that deviate by about two hours earlier or later than the average. However, individuals with extreme chronotypes may experience significant challenges in adhering to societal norms for work, school, or social activities. When these tendencies are so pronounced that they interfere with normal functioning, the individual may be diagnosed with a circadian rhythm sleep disorder. In the 20th century, there was a surge in research on sleep and biological rhythms. Nathaniel Kleitman, a physiology professor, made significant contributions to the field with his book Sleep and Wakefulness (1939, revised in 1963), where he proposed the concept of a basic rest-activity cycle. Kleitman, along with his students William C. Dement and Eugene Aserinsky, continued to advance sleep research throughout the century. Modern research into chronotypes began with O. Öquist's 1970 thesis, Charting Individual Circadian Rhythms, at the University of Göteborg, Sweden. Öquist's work was further developed by O. Östberg, who, in collaboration with J.A. Horne, created the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) in 1976. The MEQ remains a widely used tool in chronotype research, with subsequent studies validating its use across different cultures and age groups. Other assessment tools have also been developed, such as the Circadian Type Inventory (1987), the Composite Morningness Questionnaire (1989), the Lark-Owl Chronotype Indicator (1999), and the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (2003). These tools are often tailored for specific contexts, such as shift work, jet lag, athletic performance, or optimizing the timing of medical procedures. Most individuals fall somewhere between the extremes of morningness and eveningness, with estimates suggesting that up to half of the population identifies as either morning or evening types. People with similar chronotypes tend to exhibit comparable patterns in sleep, appetite, exercise, and other daily activities. For example, Horne and Östberg (1976) found that morning types have a higher daytime body temperature with an earlier peak, go to bed earlier, and wake up earlier, though sleep duration does not differ significantly between chronotypes. They also noted that age influences chronotype assessments, as a bedtime of 11:30 PM might indicate a morning type among students but an evening type in middle-aged adults. Other studies have provided additional insights into chronotype characteristics. Clodoré et al. (1986) observed differences in alertness between morning and evening types following sleep reduction. Gibertini et al. (1999) found that the timing of melatonin peaks (acrophase) is strongly associated with chronotype, with morning types showing a faster decline in melatonin levels after the peak. Duffy et al. (1999) reported that while evening types wake later in terms of clock time, morning types wake later in their circadian phase, meaning the interval between their circadian phase and wake time is longer. Baehr et al. (2000) discovered that the minimum body temperature occurs around 4:00 AM for morning types and 6:00 AM for evening types, with evening types also exhibiting lower nocturnal temperatures. This temperature minimum tends to occur earlier in women than in men. Zavada et al. (2005) suggested that the midpoint of sleep on free days is a reliable marker for chronotype, correlating well with physiological indicators like dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) and cortisol rhythm minima. They also noted that each chronotype category includes both short and long sleepers. Further research has explored the relationship between chronotypes and other traits. Giampietro and Cavallera (2006) reviewed studies linking chronotypes to personality and creative thinking. Paine et al. (2006) concluded that chronotype preference is largely independent of factors such as ethnicity, gender, and socioeconomic status, suggesting that it is primarily determined by endogenous factors.
